image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Two-panel horizontal bar chart** (ranked bar charts).
- Left panel: major sports.
- Right panel: “nonrevenue” sports.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Side-by-side panels / small multiples** by sport group (“major sports” vs. “nonrevenue” sports).
- Within each panel, bars are **not stacked**.
- Bars are **sorted/ranked** by earnings.
- A few bars in the right panel are **highlighted with color** and accompanied by an **annotation arrow/text**.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Sport | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels next to bars |
| Average earnings | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis |
| Sport group (major sports vs. “nonrevenue” sports) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into left and right panels; panel titles |
| Highlighted sports status | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of bars (red vs. light gray/white) |

Notes:
- The highlighted bars correspond to specific sports visible in the right panel, but the visualization encodes this primarily through **color**, not a separate legend.
- The annotation text and arrow are explanatory callouts, not additional plotted data variables.

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: Sports They Play, But What About the Pay?
    
    What do you notice?
    I noticed that there is a massive pay gap between athletes in major sports and those in non-revenue sports. The highest-paying major sport is men's basketball, at over $600,000, while the highest-paying nonrevenue sport is men's golf, at just over $20,000. I also noticed that while women's and men's basketball are both major sports, women get paid over $500,000 less than men. This shows that the gender pay gap is also relevant to college sports. The final thing I noticed is that women's and men's track/cross-country pay increased because of the Olympics. 
    
    What do you wonder?
    I wonder why some sports have higher pay for men than others for women. Why is the gap between major and nonrevenue sports so extreme? Are these earnings based on media attention? Why didn't any other sports, such as women's gymnastics, increase pay after the Olympics life track/cross country? 
    
    How does this relate to you and your community?
    This relates to me and my community because my friends and I all play sports, and I know some of them want to play in college. It's interesting to see the average pay between different sports like women's tennis and women's soccer, for example.

I wonder why men's basketball makes so much more money than women's basketball, and if possible added exposure to women's basketball can help even out the average earnings between the two.  This relates to me and my community because my family watches men's college basketball, and have been to many games.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph analyzes the earnings of college athletes in both major revenue sports and non-revenue sports. The major revenue sports, which include men's basketball, football, baseball, and women's basketball, show a significant pay gap between men and women, with men’s basketball earning much more than women’s basketball. In contrast, on the non-revenue side, men’s golf stands out as the highest-earning non-revenue sport, even though it doesn’t generate nearly as much revenue as the major sports. Women's gymnastics earns much more than men’s gymnastics, and men’s and women’s track and cross-country sports are on the rise in earnings, largely due to increased exposure from the Olympics. Fencing, on the other hand, generates the least revenue of all the sports listed. I wonder why softball, which is often considered the counterpart to baseball, is classified as a non-revenue sport while baseball is a major sport. I also wonder how the earnings of these sports have changed over time and if the financial gap between men’s and women’s sports will continue to persist as women’s sports gain more exposure. Additionally, I wonder how increased media coverage and sponsorship deals have influenced the revenue disparity. This graph is relevant to my community because college sports are widely followed, and this analysis offers a new perspective on how these athletes are compensated.
    Headline: The Financial Divide in College Sports

In this graph comparing the earnings of nonrevenue and revenue college sports, I noticed a couple of huge differences. First, men's basketball earns an average of $600,000, which is 200x larger than the average earnings of fencing, which is around $3,000. Then, I also noticed the NAIA was only passed 5 years ago, meaning all of this money has shot up to rapid numbers in such a short period. Finally, I saw that women's basketball brings in almost $200,000 less than men's basketball; however, many women's sports on the nonrevenue side "beat" men's sports in earnings. I am curious what caused these earnings to skyrocket so quickly in the last five years, and what brings in the most money to these groups. I also wonder if any other sports will experience growth like track and field did because of the coverage from the Olympics (if so, what sport?). This relates to me because as a student-athlete I am surrounded by the environment of people committing to specific colleges, which comes with potential financial earnings.

comments.raw_comment: The graphs display the average earnings in both major and minor sports for college student-athletes. I also noticed that the sports that are considered “major” are only basketball (for both men and women) along with baseball and football. This makes me wonder why they are the only major sports and other ones like soccer, volleyball, and lacrosse are not considered major sports. Those may be considered major because they are very popular, draw big crowds to college games, or are just the most fun to watch. This relates to my community and myself because it shows me what sports are considered majors and which aren’t in colleges. I also see many local basketball teams around my area signifying how popular of a sport it is. A title for this graph can be: “Major college sports: show me the money”
